Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette: Carmen Hernandez had always been a meticulous person, but since her divorce five years ago, her attention to detail had become an all-consuming force in her life. As a physical therapist, she took pride in creating a calm and organized environment for her patients, but at home, her need for control had grown into a compulsive cleaning habit. Every evening, after a long day of work, Carmen would spend hours reorganizing her kitchen cabinets, dusting every surface, and scrubbing the floors until they shone like new. She couldn't explain why she felt such an overwhelming urge to clean, but it made her feel safe, like she was warding off some unseen threat. Carmen's childhood had been marked by physical abuse at the hands of her caregiver. The memories were fragmented and often felt unreal, as if they belonged to someone else. Sometimes, Carmen would recall a specific incident - the sound of footsteps outside her bedroom door, the feeling of being pinned against the wall - but it was always accompanied by a strange numbness, as if she was observing herself from afar. Other times, memories would surface suddenly, without warning: a glimpse of a hand raised in anger, the smell of cheap perfume. These flashbacks left Carmen breathless and disoriented, wondering what other secrets her mind might be keeping. As an adult, Carmen had learned to navigate these memory fragments by avoiding anything that could trigger them. She avoided crowded public spaces, turned down social invitations, and stuck to a rigid routine at work. But even in ordinary situations, she felt a creeping sense of unease. Strangers approaching her on the street made her heart racing, and she always sought out a spot with her back against the wall, where she could see everyone around her. At night, Carmen would wake up multiple times to check whether she was safe - that the doors were locked, that no one was lurking in the shadows. Food had also become a source of comfort for Carmen. When she felt anxious or overwhelmed, she would turn to eating as a way to calm herself down. Her diet consisted mainly of comfort foods - pasta, pizza, fried chicken - and she often found herself devouring entire meals without even realizing it. The weight gain that followed only added to her feelings of shame and self-doubt. Despite her best efforts to keep these symptoms at bay, Carmen's life was beginning to unravel. She had started to turn down patients who required home visits, fearing the uncertainty of new environments. Her relationships with friends and family were strained, as they struggled to understand why she couldn't simply "snap out" of her anxiety. At work, Carmen felt like an imposter, as if she was just pretending to be a capable therapist while secretly drowning in her own fears. The final straw came when Carmen's daughter, Maria, announced that she was getting married and wanted her mother to give a speech at the wedding reception. The thought of standing up in front of all those strangers, with no wall to hide behind, sent Carmen into a panic. She realized then that she couldn't keep living like this - constantly on edge, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. With a heavy heart, Carmen made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to finally confront the memories and fears that had been holding her back for so long.
